The FOMC’s statement is cautiously positive on current conditions (strong labor market, solid household spending) but highlights notable downside risks: weak business fixed investment and exports, and inflation running below 2%. The weakness in investment is consistent with evidence that firms’ investment—especially inventories—is sensitive to internal funds and financing conditions (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994), which in business-cycle models can presage slower output. With market-based inflation compensation low and surveys little changed, New Keynesian analyses emphasizing expectations and the output gap (e.g., Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido; Rudebusch) support preemptive easing to keep inflation near target (Svensson). Empirical VAR work (Sims) and optimizing-policy studies (McCallum and Nelson, 1999) suggest that lowering the policy rate and providing liquidity via T-bill purchases and repos can transmit through the liquidity effect to support activity. Net tone: mildly positive on the present, dovish about risks.
